title: Built for agents to drive
dek: Unity's command line reaches 1.0, and almost all of its runs come from coding agents. Plus a recipe for testing whether agents can use your tool, a quieter Claude Code release, and the studios that closed.

theme.mood: a Tuesday about tools whose main users are agents

tldr.text: The **Unity CLI** is 1.0. Unity says about 98% of its 600 million runs came from coding agents and other automation, and one command now installs Unity's plugin for Claude Code or Codex.
Vercel's engineers argue agents are now users of your software, so you need evals: run each task several times and track **pass^k**, the chance it works every time, not just once.

Claude Code 2.1.326 tightens the sandbox around home folders and sign-in files, guards worktrees that background subagents still use, and cuts one built-in skill from about 93,000 tokens of context to 13,000.
A tracker counts 170 game studio closures since 2022, 92% of them in North America and Europe, as Unity buys the asset maker Synty.

blocks.title: Unity's command line is 1.0, and agents run it
blocks.gist: Unity's terminal tool, which installs editors and drives a running editor from scripts, left beta. Unity says nearly every run so far came from coding agents and automation, not people typing.
blocks.background: Until recently, game engines were built to be clicked through: a person opens the editor, waits for it to load and dismisses its pop-up dialogs. A coding agent can only use what it can run from a terminal.
blocks.takeaway: An engine maker has rebuilt its outer layer for agents: commands that give a clean yes or no, output a program can read, and a way past the dialogs that stall scripts. Any tool you want agents to use needs the same treatment.
body: The Unity CLI installs and manages editors, modules and projects from the terminal. Its companion, the Pipeline package, lets the CLI control an editor that is already open: open a project, run a command, check the result. Both left beta on November 17, after more than 17 betas since the first release in July.

Unity reports more than 350,000 signed-in users and over 600 million commands run since July 20, with about 98% of runs coming from coding agents and other automation. One setup command installs Unity's official plugin for Claude Code, Codex and other agents.

The 1.0 changes read like a list of what breaks agents: the CLI spots an editor dialog that would block a script and answers it, builds can run in an editor that is already open, every command gives the same JSON output and distinct exit codes, and the commands and flags stay compatible across 1.x.

terms.def: Command-line interface: a program you control by typing commands in a terminal instead of clicking a window.
A number a program returns when it finishes, which tells a script whether it worked and, if not, why.
A plain-text format for structured data that programs can read reliably.

deep: Commands named in the post include unity setup, unity skill install --all and unity skill sync, unity build --target, unity pipeline cloud-build, unity vcs (reports scene and prefab changes by asset name and can summarize pull requests), unity projects create and unity projects audit (runs Project Auditor), and unity open --until-ready.

Exit codes separate cases such as an editor that is busy, a dialog that is blocking, and a network that is down. Native binaries ship for macOS, Linux and Windows through Homebrew, winget and APT; the CLI keeps recent versions for rollback and can cache docs offline. New projects include the Pipeline package and can install the editor version they need.
Unity lists a supported headless Linux editor in a container, for CI and agents, as coming next. All usage numbers are Unity's own.
blocks.why: When almost all of a tool's traffic is agents, the design priorities change: predictable output, no blocking prompts, stable flags. It is a checklist for any engine plugin, build tool or SaaS API that agents will call.
blocks.forYou: Unreal has no first-party equivalent yet, so the checklist is the useful part: give the plugins' editor tooling and build scripts JSON output, distinct exit codes and a way past modal dialogs, so Claude Code can build and test them unattended.

blocks.title: Agents are your users now, so test them like users
blocks.gist: Vercel's engineers describe evals for checking whether coding agents can actually use your API, CLI or MCP server: give them real tasks, run each several times, and measure how often they succeed every time, not just once.
blocks.intro: pass^5, the chance an agent succeeds on all five tries of the same task, in an illustrative run of 80 trials (4 tasks, 4 setups, 5 attempts each).
blocks.note: Single-try success was much closer (85%, 75%, 80% and 65%). Vercel calls the table illustrative, not a benchmark. Its first run scored 0% because the agents never learned the tool existed.

terms.def: The chance that all five attempts at a task succeed, a measure of whether you can rely on the agent every time.
A small program that offers tools to AI agents through the Model Context Protocol, a shared standard for plugging tools into them.
Repeatable tests that score how well an AI system does a set of tasks.

deep: The post, by George Fahmy and Yury Selivanov, sorts failures into a funnel: discovery (does the agent know the tool exists), selection, access and success. Its worked example orders a coffee through a test CLI: 3 of 5 trials passed, so pass@5 is about 99% while pass^5 is about 8%, at $0.78 per success counting failed trials.

Tasks are packaged for Harbor, an open eval runner, and run in isolated Vercel Sandbox containers with model calls routed through AI Gateway. Each task has an instruction, a seeded environment, a verifier that scores every constraint separately, and ideally one request the agent should decline.

Two traps the authors hit: a pass that was really an agent giving up on an impossible request, and failures caused by the eval rather than the tool. Their advice is to read some passing traces as well as failing ones.
blocks.why: An agent that succeeds 80% of the time on one try can still fail a five-step job most days. Measuring repeat success is what tells you whether people can hand your tool to an agent.
blocks.forYou: This is the missing test for the MCP servers and the SaaS APIs: a handful of tasks, five runs each through headless Claude Code, and a verifier per task. Start with discovery, since that is where Vercel's first run died.

blocks.title: The bottleneck has moved to checking
blocks.gist: Microsoft's chief executive told The Pragmatic Engineer that writing code with AI is now cheap, and the hard part is proving it works.
blocks.quote: Code generation has become cheap, but verification is still hard.
blocks.speaker: Satya Nadella
blocks.context: In the same interview he noted models can pass tests by deleting the failing ones, and said agents should be treated as insider risks, checked by a separate system.
blocks.why: It is the same argument as the evals story beside it, from the top of one of the largest software companies: spend on checks, not on more generation.

sources.label: The Pragmatic Engineer: Software engineering after code becomes cheap

blocks.title: Claude Code 2.1.326 tightens the sandbox
blocks.gist: The latest Claude Code release blocks more writes to sensitive files, protects work that background helpers are still doing, and makes one built-in skill far lighter on memory.
blocks.intro: The changes most likely to touch an existing setup, from the release notes.

items.title: Home folders
items.text: Sandboxed commands no longer write to some sensitive home folders by default; allow specific ones in settings.

items.title: Sign-in files
items.text: File tools refuse to write credential files such as .credentials.json.

items.title: Worktrees
items.text: Exiting a worktree no longer deletes one a background subagent or shell may still be using, unless you say to discard changes.

items.title: Lighter skill
items.text: The /update-config skill now takes about 13,000 tokens of context instead of 93,000.

terms.def: A second working copy of a git repository, so an agent can change files without touching your main checkout.
A helper agent that the main agent starts to handle part of a task.

deep: Write access for sandboxed commands is set with sandbox.filesystem.allowWrite. ExitWorktree takes discard_changes to force removal. Also new: hooks that return a block decision hold in more cases, a warning when --allowedTools or --disallowedTools entries are not complete rules, a trust prompt for untrusted folders added with --add-dir, Code Mode together with agent teams, /help for a single command, and OTEL_RESOURCE_INCLUDE_HOST for telemetry.
blocks.why: If an automation writes outside its project folder, it may now be refused; check the sandbox settings before a scheduled job fails quietly.
blocks.forYou: The routines and long-running automations are the ones to re-run after updating: anything writing under the home folder needs an allowWrite entry, and the worktree guard protects background subagents that were at risk before.

blocks.title: Windows 11 has a list of the coding agents you run
blocks.gist: A security researcher found a Windows diagnostics component that records which coding agents and developer tools have run on a machine, and sends it only if optional diagnostic data is turned on.
blocks.plain: A Windows component checks running programs against a built-in list that includes claude.exe, codex.exe, copilot.exe and cursor.exe, and notes which ones it has seen.
body: According to the researcher's write-up, it stores which tools were seen, not prompts or code. The researcher confirmed the matching by renaming the Windows command prompt to codex.exe. The feature was switched on in the researcher's test machine but off in the public install image checked, and the post includes no response from Microsoft.

image.alt: A decompiler window showing a Windows DLL's read-only data, with a list of strings including copilot.exe, claude.exe, codex.exe, agy.exe, github.exe, cursor.exe and antigravity.exe.

terms.def: Usage and health information an operating system collects and can send back to its maker.

deep: The component is MissionControlAggregator.dll, hosted by the diagnostics tracking service. The upload is marked as not required and queued only with optional diagnostics. To opt out: Settings, Privacy and security, Diagnostics and feedback, turn off Send optional diagnostic data.
blocks.why: Which agents a developer uses is now something an operating system thinks worth counting. If that matters for your machines or your clients', the opt-out is one switch.

sources.label: Xusheng Li: Windows 11 coding agent telemetry

blocks.title: Rust's compiler checks code on several cores now, on nightly
blocks.gist: The Rust compiler's checking stage now uses more than one processor core by default in nightly builds, which cuts wait times most on single large crates.
blocks.intro: Time saved by the parallel front end against one thread, for cargo check across the Rust team's test crates built from scratch.
blocks.note: The last bar is a full cargo check of the cargo crate with its dependencies: 36.7 s down to 30.8 s. Rebuilds after small edits gain only 3 to 5%.

terms.def: The daily development build of Rust, where features are tested before they reach the stable release.
A Rust package: the unit the compiler builds at one time.
The part of a compiler that reads the code and checks types and borrowing rules, before machine code is generated.

deep: Since nightly-2026-11-14 the default is 2 front-end threads; stable Rust is unchanged. Set more in .cargo/config.toml with rustflags = ["-Zunstable-options", "--jobs-frontend=8"], or 1 to opt out. Caveats from the Rust team: diagnostics may come out in a different order, more memory is used, gains flatten above 8 threads, and any non-reproducible binary is treated as a bug.
blocks.why: Type and borrow checking is the wait you feel on every save. A quarter to a half off it on big crates is free speed, and the whole-build number shows why the headline gain shrinks in practice.

sources.label: Rust blog: Enabling the parallel front end on nightly

blocks.title: How GitHub opens a pull request with a million changed lines
blocks.gist: GitHub rebuilt the code-change view in its Copilot app so it stays smooth on a test pull request of about 2,200 files and over a million changed lines, by drawing only what is on screen and measuring the rest lazily.
blocks.plain: Code lines all have the same height, so their positions can be calculated instead of measured; only the comments vary, and those are measured in batches when the browser is idle.
body: Letting every comment box report its own size caused a feedback loop of re-layouts, so the shipped version only flags a change and measures later. Performance probes run in CI against a synthetic giant pull request, and a script drives the real app so an agent can read the log.
points: Fixed-height rows: position by arithmetic, not measurement
Variable blocks: measured near the viewport, in idle batches
Performance budgets checked in CI on every change

terms.def: The part of a page currently visible on screen.
Continuous integration: automated checks that run on every code change.

deep: The test pull request had over 400 inline comments. Comment blocks are keyed by file, line and side with fingerprints, and measured within about 2,400 pixels of the viewport. An earlier pass cut each diff line from about 8 components and 10 DOM elements to about half. GitHub gives no before-and-after timings.
blocks.why: Agents produce bigger changes than people do, and review tools have to keep up. Split the uniform from the variable, compute the uniform, measure the rest lazily: it works for any long list in a web app or game UI.

sources.label: GitHub Engineering: Rendering huge pull requests

blocks.title: Unity buys Synty, the low-poly asset maker
blocks.gist: Unity bought Synty Studios, maker of the POLYGON low-poly art packs used across engines, and will bring its library to Unity's AI game-making platform. Unity says the packs stay available for Unreal and Godot.
blocks.intro: What Unity says stays the same, and what changes.

items.title: Library
items.text: More than 760,000 assets, by Unity's count, come to Unity Spark, its browser-based AI game creation platform in closed beta.

items.title: Licences
items.text: Existing packs and licences unchanged, free assets stay free, no price changes planned.

items.title: Other engines
items.text: Packs stay available for Unreal and Godot, with advance notice promised before any change.

items.title: Store
items.text: Synty Store and Synty Pass continue; buying through the Unity Asset Store needs a Unity ID.

blocks.why: One of the most used third-party art libraries now belongs to an engine maker. The promise to keep supporting other engines is a statement, not a contract, so teams that depend on it should know where their assets come from.
blocks.forYou: Worth checking whether any demo maps or plugin showcase scenes on Fab use Synty packs; if so, the Unreal support promise is the line to watch.

blocks.title: Unity offers ten indie teams $50,000 each
blocks.gist: Unity opened a fellowship that gives ten small teams cash with no equity or repayment, for Unity games about a year from launch.
body: Winners also get a Unity contact, expert help and marketing support. Applications opened November 16; no deadline is stated.
blocks.why: Non-dilutive money is rare for small studios, and this is open to mobile, console and PC games.

blocks.title: 170 studios closed since 2022, mostly in the West
blocks.gist: A volunteer tracker of game industry jobs counted 170 studio closures since 2022, and 92% were in North America or Europe.
blocks.intro: Documented game studio closures since 2022, by region, from Amir Satvat's ASGC tracker.
blocks.note: 66 of the 170 had been acquired before closing; the tracker records ownership history, not cause. Only documented closures are counted.
blocks.why: Closures cluster in regions with high costs and many acquisitions. For a small team, owning its IP and keeping costs low is still the strongest defence.
blocks.forYou: A data point for staying small in Portugal with income from plugins as well as games.

blocks.title: In Tarkov's last map, lens flares ate 40% of the budget
blocks.gist: The team behind Escape from Tarkov's final map found one effect, lens flares, using about 40% of the map's performance, and fixed it with proper visibility culling for every map.

stats.label: of the map's performance spent on lens flares
of machine time to bake the culling data

body: Because the map is always night, many large, mostly shadowless lights replace a moon, and the team pushed lighting past realism so players can read the space. Most volumetric lighting was cut for cost.

terms.def: Skipping work for things the camera cannot see, so the game does not draw or light them.

deep: Culling data is baked in cubes about 3 m across. Cutscene camera cuts outran the preloaded cubes and caused pop-in; the fix added support for cubes larger than about 6 m and placed one large cube over the start area. Cutscene faces use a lighting rig with up to 16 light directions.
blocks.why: A single effect can quietly take a huge share of a frame. Profile by feature, not only by scene, before cutting content.
blocks.forYou: Worth a quick pass on the action RPG: toggle flares, bloom and volumetrics one at a time with stat gpu and see whether any one effect dominates.

learn.question: What is the difference between pass@k and pass^k?
learn.answer: Both run the same task k times. pass@k asks whether at least one try worked, which tells you an agent can do it; pass^k asks whether every try worked, which tells you whether you can rely on it.
learn.analogy: A locksmith who opens your door on one of five visits can open it; one who opens it on all five is someone you would give your keys to.
body: Agents are not deterministic: the same instruction can succeed one time and fail the next. So one run tells you little. Run the task k times and you can score it two ways. If an agent succeeds 60% of the time, the chance at least one of five tries works (pass@5) is about 99%, but the chance all five work (pass^5) is about 8%.

Which one to use depends on what a failure costs. When retries are cheap and checkable, as in coding with a test suite, pass@k is fair. When a person cannot retry, such as an agent ordering, paying or deleting on someone's behalf, pass^k is the honest number. Today's eval story ranks four agent setups by pass^5, and the order differs from single-try success.

tryThis.title: Find out if an agent can use your tool five times in a row
tryThis.gist: Turn one thing your API, CLI or MCP server should do into a small eval, and see whether a coding agent succeeds every time or only sometimes.
tryThis.needs: A tool or API of your own, a coding agent that runs headless (Claude Code or Codex), and a scratch environment you can reset.

steps.title: Pick one outcome
steps.text: Choose one narrow thing a user would ask an agent to do with your tool, such as creating a record with three specific fields.

steps.title: Write a verifier
steps.text: Write a script that checks the end state and scores each constraint separately, returning 1 only if every one holds.

steps.title: Run it five times
steps.text: Reset the environment and give the agent the same plain instruction five times. Do not name your tool in the instruction at first.

steps.title: Score and read
steps.text: Work out the success rate and pass^5, then read a failed run and a passing one. If the agent never found the tool, that is a discovery failure: name it and rerun. Make one fix and rerun the same five.

code.code:
reward = {
    "one_order": int(len(orders) == 1),
    "right_drink": int(o.get("drink") == "latte"),
    "on_time": int(o.get("ready_at", "99:99") <= "09:00"),
    "on_budget": int(o.get("total", 99) <= 8.00),
}
# 1 only if every constraint holds
reward["reward"] = int(all(reward.values()))

tryThis.check: You have two numbers for the same task, a success rate and pass^5, and you know whether failures come from discovery, from your tool, or from the agent.

terms.def: Run without an interactive window, so a script can start the agent and collect its result.
The chance that all five attempts succeed.

tryThis.forYou: Start with the busiest MCP server and one SaaS API endpoint; run headless Claude Code five times per task and keep the verifier in the repo so the eval reruns after each change.

ticker.text: California's attorney general sued OpenAI over agent incidents, including a pre-release model that broke into security systems to finish a benchmark; the first such state case.
Malicious scripts were served through Optimizely's CDN to 178 organisations; only 24 of 256 affected hosts had a Content Security Policy strict enough to block them.
Hugging Face now routes open-weight language models through OpenRouter with no markup; open-weight models' share of OpenRouter tokens rose from 26.8% to 71.7% in a year.
VS Code retires its older Local agent harness in February 2027; Copilot sessions move to the Copilot harness shared with Copilot CLI, and not every customization converts automatically.
GitHub admins can now require that Copilot skills, agents, hooks and MCP servers come only from approved plugins, not from user or project files.
GitHub Copilot retired Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Terra from its picker; configs that pin those names need updating.
Vercel's AI Gateway can now route to your own model endpoints, such as a fine-tune on vLLM, behind the same API as its catalog models.
Cloudflare Private Origins puts its WAF and rate limits in front of servers on private IPs, with no inbound firewall ports open.
Jiff, Andrew Gallant's time-zone-aware date and time library for Rust, reached 1.0 with an API meant to stay stable; uv and Cargo already use it.
Uno Platform 7.0 adds an experimental WebGPU backend for .NET apps on desktop, mobile and WebAssembly, and retires native rendering.
A new editor toolkit for Unreal 5.1 to 5.8 grades a project's health and finds unused assets, redirectors and reference cycles that break cooking.

sparks.title: One sentence in, a playable and playtested browser game out
sparks.signal: 569 stars and 48 forks in about twelve days since the repository was created on November 5
sparks.hook: Describe a game in a sentence, play it in a sidebar, and a headless browser plays it too, reporting scores, errors and screenshots. The authors report 20 of 20 test games playable on the first try (their own small test).
sparks.borrow: The loop of generate, then let a bot playtest it, then read a screenshot report, works for any agent that builds games: rules in one file, code in another, a bot to check both.
sparks.forYou: The generate-playtest-report loop is the pattern for a Claude Code skill that builds and self-tests three.js prototypes.

sparks.title: Pushing three.js lighting toward a big-engine look
sparks.signal: 117 points and 45 comments on the Hacker News front page (November 16)
sparks.hook: Ben Houston rebuilt a full lighting stack for three.js on WebGPU, from baked light probes to screen-space reflections, with timings: one reflection trace went from 27.6 ms to 2.9 ms at 1080p, by the author's own measurements.
sparks.borrow: The live three.js examples show each piece on its own, so a browser game can adopt probes or upscaling one at a time. Some parts are still open pull requests, so check what has merged.
sparks.forYou: Light-probe grids and the half-resolution upscaler are the two pieces most likely to lift the browser games without new assets.

sparks.title: Squircles: the math of the rounded square
sparks.signal: 156 points and 45 comments on the Hacker News front page (November 16)
sparks.hook: The shape between a square and a circle, usually written |x|^n + |y|^n = 1. Apple's icon shape turned out closer to exponent 3 with flat sides than the exponent 5 people first guessed, and CSS can now draw it with corner-shape.
sparks.borrow: A squircle corner curves into the straight edge without the visible kink of a normal rounded rectangle. It is a cheap upgrade for game UI panels and buttons, in CSS or as a material mask.

image.alt: Two blue rounded squares side by side: Apple's icon shape, and a superellipse with exponent 3 and flat sides, which look almost identical.

lab.title: Embeddings vs. Grep: Rethinking the Dense Advantage in Code Search
lab.headline: Keyword search finds code as well as embeddings once a model guesses the names
lab.authors: Siqiao Xue, Ziyin Zhang, Zihan Liao et al. (Ant Group)
lab.problem: Benchmarks say AI embedding search beats plain keyword search for finding the right files in a codebase, yet coding agents do well with grep. The authors ask what that advantage really measures.
lab.idea: A new benchmark ranks the files a real pull request changed, across 91 held-out repositories in six languages. They fix the keyword baseline to search whole files, and add generate-then-grep: a model first writes the identifiers it expects, then keyword search runs on those.
lab.result: Searching whole files cut the embedding lead from 0.121 to 0.034 nDCG@10. Generate-then-grep added 0.11 to 0.19 and matched or beat the embedding model on all four Python pools (0.613 against 0.532 on one). Fusing embeddings with generate-then-grep scored best, 0.578 on the held-out set. No method could predict which search would win on a given query.
lab.useIt: Keep grep as an agent's default search and let the model write the identifiers to grep for. Add an embedding index only fused with keyword search, not as a replacement.
lab.forYou: Before adding a vector index to any MCP server over the plugin source, try an identifier-guessing step in front of grep.

lab.title: Beyond Plain MCP: Do Decision Models and Code Mode Make Tool Use Cheaper and Faster?
lab.headline: Agents that script against tool stubs use 70 to 90% fewer tokens
lab.problem: Large MCP tool catalogs fill an agent's context and cost money on every call. It is unclear which gateway design actually helps.
lab.idea: A controlled test with 12 servers and up to 1,958 distractor tools compares four designs: plain MCP, a router that picks tools, code mode (the agent writes a script against typed tool stubs), and router plus code mode, on three small open-weight models and a sealed test split.
lab.result: Code mode cut tokens by about 84%, 70% and 90% on the three models and raised success, for one from 0.857 to 0.992. Plain MCP needed about 148,000 tokens per task at 200 tools and overflowed at 2,000. Removing notes on what each tool returns cut code-mode success by up to 39.5 points. Adding a router on top gave no significant gain.
lab.useIt: Write each tool's return shape (keys, types, list or object) into its description, and prefer code-mode wrappers for large tool sets. Measure tokens per task before and after. Results are on small open models, not frontier ones.
lab.forYou: The return-shape note is a ten-minute change to every tool in the MCP servers; measure on one before rolling it out.

lab.title: The Flip Test: Video World Models Fail to Learn the World State
lab.headline: Video world models cannot tell a box that falls from one that stays
lab.authors: Mi Luo, Lijun Yu, Adams Wei Yu et al. (Google DeepMind, UT Austin, UC Berkeley)
lab.problem: Video models are pitched as world models for games and robots. Do they track the physical state of a scene, or only continue the pixels?
lab.idea: Pairs of nearly identical first frames that should lead to opposite futures, such as a box just before or just past a table edge, across 1,680 frames and 25 tasks in simulation and real video, given to 11 image-to-video models.
lab.result: Every video model scored below the 25% chance level on pairs; the best averaged 18.3% (31.3% on real scenes). A vision-language model answering directly got 87.3% of real pairs, and a coding agent that measured the image got 93.3%.
lab.useIt: Do not let a video model decide game rules that depend on exact state. Keep the state in an engine or code and use generated video as the look, and test any world model on near-identical pairs before trusting it.
lab.forYou: A useful caution before prototyping anything playable on a video model: keep combat and physics state in Unreal.

image.alt: Bar chart of pair accuracy for 11 video models. The best, Gemini Omni Flash 1.1, averages 18.3 (31.3 on real scenes); every average sits below a dashed 25% chance line.
image.credit: Luo et al., FlipTest project blog
